Vandenberg SLC-4E, 2021-11-24. DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) was the first dedicated planetary-defense mission — a kinetic impactor designed to demonstrate that a small spacecraft hitting an asteroid hard enough could measurably change its orbit, a technique that could deflect a real impact threat with sufficient lead time.
Falcon 9 second stage delivers DART onto an Earth-trailing heliocentric trajectory targeting the Didymos binary system.
First major mid-course correction. Cumulative ion-thruster firings during cruise demonstrate the NEXT-C electric propulsion subsystem.

2022-09-26. DART enters the gravitational sphere of the Didymos binary asteroid system. SMART Nav (Small-body Maneuvering Autonomous Real Time Navigation) takes over targeting from ground control 4 hours before impact — the spacecraft must autonomously distinguish Dimorphos (160-m moonlet) from Didymos (780-m parent) and hit the smaller of the two.

23:14 UTC, 2022-09-26. DART struck Dimorphos at ~6.6 km/s. Final images from DRACO camera resolved boulders on the surface in the last few seconds. The 611-kg spacecraft delivered ~11 GJ of kinetic energy. Orbital-period change measured from Earth: 33 minutes shorter (~4.6% reduction in Dimorphos's 11.9-hour orbit around Didymos), exceeding the 73-second success threshold by ~25× — the momentum-transfer enhancement factor β ≈ 3.6 indicates significant momentum carry from ejected surface material. First demonstration that humans can move an asteroid.

DART transmitted nominal telemetry up to ~3 seconds before impact, then loss of signal as expected. The CubeSat LICIACube (deployed 15 days before impact) flew past about 57 km from Dimorphos, imaging the impact plume in real time. Hubble Space Telescope imaged the ejecta tail in the days that followed; the JWST also observed the impact.
First demonstration of kinetic-impactor planetary defense; first time humans moved an asteroid

DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) was the first planetary-defense mission ever flown — a 611-kg spacecraft sent to hit a 160-m asteroid hard enough to change its orbit. The target was Dimorphos, a moonlet of the 780-m asteroid Didymos. Launched 2021-11-24 on a Falcon 9; the SMART Nav autonomous navigation system took over 4 hours before impact to distinguish Dimorphos from its parent and target the smaller body. Impact 2022-09-26 at 23:14 UTC at ~6.6 km/s. Measured orbital-period change: 33 minutes (~4.6%), exceeding the 73-second success threshold by ~25×. Momentum-transfer enhancement factor β ≈ 3.6 indicated significant carry from ejected surface material. The CubeSat LICIACube observed the plume; HST imaged the resulting ejecta tail for weeks; JWST observed the impact. First demonstration that humans can move an asteroid.
23:14 UTC. ~6.6 km/s. 33-min orbital-period change — first deflection of an asteroid by humans.
